summary.en: How a judo contest is won, scored and penalised, in one page, with the three scores now in use: ippon, waza-ari and yuko. A summary of the essentials; your federation's current rulebook is always the authority.

prose.en: Rules change more often than techniques do, and the scoring is where they change most. Yuko was taken out of international judo in 2017 and brought back for the current Olympic cycle, so a contest now has three scores again and the coach shouting from the mat side may be working from any of the last three rulebooks. This page covers the shape of a contest under current international (IJF) rules so a newcomer or a grading candidate can follow one; where it disagrees with your federation's current rulebook, the rulebook wins.

A contest runs four minutes, for seniors, juniors and cadets alike, and is won by ippon: a throw landing largely on the back with control, speed and force; twenty seconds of hold-down; or submission to a strangle or an elbow lock. Two waza-ari make ippon and end it the same way, and so does a third shido against the other contestant. If time runs out with nothing decisive, the higher score wins: more waza-ari first, and if the waza-ari are level, more yuko. Only if the contestants are level on both does the contest go into golden score.

Ippon ends the contest. Waza-ari is the throw that lands past ninety degrees of the shoulder axis but not on the back, or that misses one of the four elements of ippon - speed, force, on the back, controlled to the landing. Yuko is the smallest score: a landing on the side at about ninety degrees or further forward, on the upper back, on the side across shoulder and one elbow or hand, on one or both buttocks, or on the neck. There is no score at all where the stomach, the front of the hip or a knee touches first. Ippon, waza-ari and yuko show on the scoreboard as 100, 10 and 1, which is the plainest statement of the rule below: no number of ones ever makes a ten.

heading.en: Scores do not add up, except two waza-ari

prose.en: Two waza-ari make ippon. Nothing else accumulates. Yuko are counted and announced - one, two, three - but they never combine into a waza-ari: ten yuko still lose to one waza-ari. This is what makes them a tie-breaker rather than a running total, and it is the part most often got wrong by anyone who learned the pre-2017 rules, where scores did build.

A contestant who bridges on the way down, taking the landing on the head and one or both feet rather than the back, is scored ippon against however well the escape works. The rule is there to stop judoka loading their own neck to save a contest, and it is one of the few places where the score turns on what the falling contestant does rather than on the throw.

Osaekomi has its own clock, started when the referee calls it and stopped by toketa or matte. Five to nine seconds scores yuko, ten to nineteen scores waza-ari, and twenty seconds is ippon and the end of the contest. A hold broken at four seconds scores nothing.

Golden score has no time limit and begins with the scores as they stand; the shido already given stay on the board. The first score of any kind wins it - a yuko is enough - and so does the other contestant's third shido. A hold-down started in golden score ends it at five seconds, on the yuko. This is the practical effect of bringing yuko back: an overtime that could once run for many minutes now ends on the first properly controlled landing on the side.

Shido punishes passivity and minor infringements: false attacks, stepping out, defensive or dangerous gripping, breaking a grip with two hands and taking nothing in return, taking hold of a leg or the trousers, and wasting time between matte and hajime by dawdling over a judogi, hair or belt. Passivity has a clock of its own: once conventional grips are taken and the exchange is otherwise progressing, forty-five seconds without an attack draws a shido. Three shido make hansoku-make. Direct hansoku-make is kept for the gravest acts, among them kawazu-gake, kani-basami, do-jime and ashi-garami, and it ends the contest at once. The leg grabs belong to the first group and not the second: they cost a shido, not the contest. Shido never score, and they decide a contest only by reaching three.

Ne-waza continues while there is progress: working towards a hold, strangle or lock. When it stalls, the referee calls matte and the contest returns to standing. Real groundwork attacks now count towards combativity exactly as standing attacks do, so a contestant who genuinely attacks on the mat is not penalised for failing to attack on their feet - though pushing and holding on is not an attack. Strangles and elbow locks are for senior age groups only; check your federation's age rules.

In IBSA (Paralympic) judo, contestants begin already gripped and are restarted in grips after each break, and the classifications group contestants by sight and experience. If you are a visually impaired judoka reading this, your contest starts at the part most others have to fight for.
